headline: Bunker Push Into Raritan Bay: Blues on the Pods, Fluke Holding the Channel Edges
subhead: With bait pouring in from Belmar and a soft neap tide easing the rips, I'm staying inside the Hook this week — here's where I'd put the boat.
body_markdown:
I made the call Sunday morning standing on the dock watching the swell roll in off the Bight — ocean side is a washing machine right now, pushing close to four feet at five seconds out past the buoy line, and that's not fishable water unless you're on a party boat hull. So the decision was easy: stay inside the Hook this week. Work the bay, work the rivers, let the ocean sort itself out on its own time.

Good thing, because the bay's got something building. Bunker schools that have been getting hammered by blues from Belmar on north are finally pushing into our end of the water. I've watched the pods thicken up off the beach between the Highlands and Sandy Hook for two days straight, and if that keeps up — and there's no reason it shouldn't with this calm, stable stretch of weather sitting on top of us — bluefish should follow those pods around the Hook and into the bay within a day or two. We flagged this exact thing last week, said the bay would settle into its summer rhythm of bait and blues and fluke on the tide, and here we are watching it happen in real time.

The first place that pattern always shows up locally is the ferry channel and the Rip at the Hook on the tide change. That's where I'd have eyes Tuesday and Wednesday morning — first light, incoming water pushing bait against the channel edge, gulls starting to work overhead. When the blues do show, don't overthink it. A 1-ounce diamond jig with a green tube tail, or a bucktail with no trailer at all, gets eaten the second it hits the wash when they're on bunker. Match the size of whatever peanut or adult bunker they're chopping and you're in business.

While we wait on that to fully develop, the fluke bite has carried the water the way it always does in late July. Sandy Hook Bay and the Reach remain the most dependable thing going right now — a daytime program on moving water, nothing fancy required. My best drifts the last two weeks have come working the channel edges off Flynn's Knoll on the last two hours of the incoming, four- to five-ounce bucktails tipped with a five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along the bottom where the sand drops into the channel. Keyport Flats has been giving up shorts by the bucket with the occasional keeper mixed in over that soft mussel bottom in 15 to 18 feet — adding a strip of squid on top of the Gulp has been the difference-maker for me when the current goes light.

Speaking of light current — today's first-quarter neap has taken some of the snap out of the rips, and that's actually working in our favor on the fluke grounds. Instead of one tight window right at max tide, the drift stays fishable through a longer stretch on either side of the swing. You don't have to be married to the exact moment the tide turns. At Flynn's Knoll and out toward Romer Shoal, that means more usable hours on the water for the same trip out.

Striped bass are the trickier piece of the puzzle right now, and I'll be straight with you — daytime bass fishing in the bay this time of year is mostly a low-percentage play. The water's carrying that heavy summer warmth, and with it the keeper-class fish have slid into a low-light and after-dark pattern, same as pretty much everywhere south of the Cape right now. If you want a real shot at a slot fish, you're fishing dawn, dusk, or full dark, working bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig around Romer Shoal and the deeper edges off the Hook, or drifting a live bunker if you can snag one out of the pods moving through. The Navesink mouth and the deeper bend by the Highlands bridge have both given up fish after dark to guys soaking eels — old-school, but it still works when the moon's this quiet.

Snapper blues are thick in the Navesink and Shrewsbury right now, which is a good problem to have if you've got a kid in the boat — small silver spoons or a sliver of bunker on a number 6 hook off any dock will keep them busy for hours. Porgies are holding steady over the reef structure off Romer Shoal and along the Highlands side, bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig in 20 to 25 feet — nothing spectacular, but a reliable box-filler on a slow bay day. Weakfish are scattered at best — a fish here and there over the Keyport Flats on soft plastics at dusk, but I wouldn't build a trip around them the way we could a decade back.

Look ahead: if the bunker keep pushing the way they have the last couple days, I expect the ferry channel and the water off Flynn's Knoll to turn into the bite everybody's chasing by the weekend. Watch the birds before anything else — they'll tell you it's happening before you see a single swirl. If the bait scatters or a wind shift breaks the pattern, don't force it; fall back on the fluke program in the Reach, because that bite isn't going anywhere with the water this stable. Either way, I'm keeping the boat inside the Hook this week and letting the ocean chop settle down before I run anything out past Romer.
